set.title: Fold performance and body storage
Profile fold apply loop
set.body: Cold fold at the 30k-event reference is ~109 ms and apply-bound (~85 ms replaying events, ~2.8 us/event; body size adds only ~8 ms). Profile the apply loop before optimizing: find whether ts parsing or per-field dict churn dominates. Measure, then decide.

set.title: Implement size-triggered body spill
set.body: Per spec section 13.2: bodies stay inline; a body exceeding a configurable threshold (default 4096 bytes) spills to bodies/<id>.md on write, and rp show resolves either form transparently. Section 5.3 already permits both shapes, so no schema change. Include a doctor check that every referenced sidecar file exists. Threshold tuning should use the by-type body percentiles from the rp stats ticket once a real corpus exists.

set.title: Set-wise three-way merge for labels
set.body: Known phase-1 gap. Labels (and other set fields) currently merge by per-field last-write-wins, which silently loses concurrent set additions from two runners. Implement set-wise three-way merge so concurrent labels+ ops compose.

set.title: rp stats command
set.body: Extend rp stats to report body-size percentiles split by ticket type (epic vs task), so the bimodal body distribution behind the section 13.2 spill decision can be observed. This supplies signals D1/D2 once a real corpus exists and tunes the 4096-byte spill threshold.

set.title: Compaction loses events if interrupted between log rewrite and archive append
set.body: src/rohrpost/compact.py run() rewrites (truncates) log.jsonl to only the kept events (_rewrite_log at :177) BEFORE appending the archived events to the archive buckets (the _append_archive loop at :178-179). A crash or SIGKILL between those two steps permanently loses the to-be-archived events: in that window they are removed from the log but not yet present in any archive file, existing only in the in-memory archive_buckets dict. Spec §6.1 specifies the crash-safe order - archive first (step 2), then rewrite the log (step 3) - which leaves only dedupable duplicates on a crash (the fold drops them by event id). Fix: append to archive files first, then rewrite the log, all still under store.file_lock. Add a regression test that simulates an interruption between the steps and asserts no events are lost.

set.title: Doctor authentication probes for all providers
set.body: rp doctor (spec §10.1) must verify remote credentials actually authenticate, not merely that a token env var is present. GitHub already has a real probe (providers/github.py + the github branch of doctor.py _remote_authenticated). The generic fallback (doctor.py _remote_authenticated, ~:206-215) only checks token presence and returns True for a present-but-invalid or expired token, so a configured non-github remote with a dead token passes the check. Each provider needs its own authentication probe in rp doctor. Tracked per provider below.

set.title: Doctor authentication probe: GitLab
set.body: Add a real authentication probe for the GitLab remote to rp doctor, so a present-but-invalid or expired token is reported as failing rather than passing. Today the generic _remote_authenticated (doctor.py, ~:206-215) only checks token presence for non-github remotes (spec audit finding #4), returning True for a dead token. Depends on the GitLab provider landing (phase 3).

set.title: Doctor authentication probe: Jira
set.body: Add a real authentication probe for the Jira remote to rp doctor, so a present-but-invalid or expired token is reported as failing rather than passing. Today the generic _remote_authenticated (doctor.py, ~:206-215) only checks token presence for non-github remotes (spec audit finding #4), returning True for a dead token. Depends on the Jira provider landing (phase 3).

set.title: Doctor authentication probe: Linear
set.body: Add a real authentication probe for the Linear remote to rp doctor, so a present-but-invalid or expired token is reported as failing rather than passing. Today the generic _remote_authenticated (doctor.py, ~:206-215) only checks token presence for non-github remotes (spec audit finding #4), returning True for a dead token. Depends on the Linear provider landing (phase 3).

set.title: Body-merge conflicts must keep conflict markers in the body
set.body: Spec §8.3 requires that on a body-merge collision the conflict markers (<<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>>) are kept IN the body and the ticket is flagged. The code computes the marker-laden three-way merge in _merge_body (merge.py ~:120-130) but then DISCARDS it, recording only the original local/remote values in a FieldConflict; _flag_conflict (sync.py ~:234-267) writes status=review + a conflict:<remote> label + a comment, but never updates the body - so the markers a human or agent needs in order to resolve the conflict are lost. The merge.py module docstring (~:17-18) already claims "keeping conflict markers on collision", which the flag path does not do. Fix: under the default flag policy, write the marker-laden merged text to the body in addition to the existing label/comment. Add coverage asserting the markers survive in the body (current tests/test_merge.py:59-64 only checks the flag, not the markers).

set.title: Human-addressable tickets: how a person points at a Rohrpost ticket
set.body:
## Destination

A locked decision on **how a human addresses a Rohrpost ticket**, recorded as an ADR plus an
amendment to spec §5.1 (Identifiers) and §10 (CLI), ready to hand to a build session. The
decision, not the code: implementation is handed off once the way is clear.

## Notes

**Domain.** Rohrpost's id/addressing ergonomics, driven by `/wayfinder` being awkward to
drive by hand: `RP-jdt9c2` is hard to type and impossible to hold in your head.

**Skills.** Call `grilling` and `domain-modeling` every session. Use `research` for facts
outside this repo. No `CONTEXT.md` exists yet — create one when the first term is resolved.

**Plan, don't do.** The destination is a decision, not shipped code.

**Standing constraints, settled while charting:**

- **Agent-first holds** (`AGENTS.md`). Human affordances live on the *input* side only — what
  `rp` accepts. What agents emit and consume does not change; `rp ready --json` stays fast
  and small (§10).
- **Ambiguity is a hard error** (`exit 1`), never a guess. Determinism is worth more to an
  agent than convenience is to a human.
- **The stored id form is fixed** at 6 lowercase base32 chars (§5.1). Only the *addressing
  layer* is in play — what `rp` accepts as input and what it renders.
- **"Hard to type" and "hard to reason about" are two problems.** Typing is input
  ergonomics. Reasoning is a rendering-and-prose problem: 6 random characters can never be
  memorable, so the fix is to keep bare ids out of the human's face, not to make them
  prettier.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket; zoom the link for the detail it holds -->

## Not yet specified

- **The write-up itself**: which ADR, and the exact §5.1 / §10 wording. Waits on the
  addressing mechanism being settled.
- **Shell completion**: whether it is part of the answer, and for which shells. None exists
  today. Waits on the moments audit.
- **A positional handle** over the last result set (`rp show @2` against `rp ready`). Waits
  on the moments audit and on the rendering question.
- **Abbreviation durability**: what happens when an abbreviation that was unique becomes
  ambiguous as tickets accumulate, and whether an abbreviation may ever be *written down*
  (commit message, ticket body, map link) rather than merely typed. Waits on the resolution
  mechanism.
- **Knock-on to the skill's own output**: whether any of this changes the link form
  `/wayfinder` writes into a map's Decisions-so-far. Waits on the map-addressing decision.

## Out of scope

- **Changing the stored id form** — sequential numbers, counters, or title-derived slugs.
  Spec §5.1 rejects these deliberately: they need either central coordination (which this
  design exists to avoid) or mutability. Reopening this would redraw the destination, and
  that is a fresh effort, not a resumption.

set.title: Which human moments actually require typing a ticket id?
set.body:
## Question

Where does a human *actually* have to produce a ticket id, and where do they only think they
do? Everything else on this map is sized by the answer, so it goes first.

The whole effort rests on the premise that humans type ids. That premise is untested. `rp`
takes `<id>` positionally on eleven commands (§10), but this repo is agent-first: most of
those calls are made by agents that just read the id out of a previous `--json` response and
never type anything. If the human's real path is `rp ready` → copy → paste, then typing is
not the problem and this map should shrink drastically.

Audit the moments and classify each one:

- **Copy-paste** — the id is already on screen from a previous command. No typing.
- **Transcribe** — the id is on screen but in a different surface (a browser, a chat message,
  the map body, a PR) and has to be retyped by hand.
- **Recall** — no id on screen at all; the human has to *know* which ticket they mean and go
  find it.

The last two are the expensive ones, and they may want different answers: transcription is a
character-accuracy problem, recall is a search problem.

Concrete moments to test, at minimum: invoking `/wayfinder` with a map; picking a ticket off
`rp ready` to claim; `rp show`-ing something a colleague or agent mentioned by name;
referring to a ticket in a commit message; jumping back to a ticket the day after.

**Resolved when** the moments are enumerated and classified, and it is clear which class the
effort is actually optimising for — including the possible answer that typing is rare enough
that only the recall path deserves work.

set.title: How comparable tools make random ids addressable
set.body:
## Question

How do comparable tools let a human address an object whose identifier is random? Rohrpost is
not the first to choose uncoordinated random ids and then have to hand them to a person, and
the prior art is unusually rich. Gather it before designing anything.

Cover at least:

- **Jujutsu (`jj`)** — the closest analogue by far. Random change ids, resolved by unique
  prefix, and it goes further: it renders the distinguishing prefix in a different colour so
  the human can see *how much* of the id they need to type, and it deliberately draws change
  ids from a different alphabet than commit hashes so the two can never be confused. Report
  the shortest-prefix rules, the ambiguity behaviour, and how prefixes are kept stable.
- **Git** — `--abbrev` / `core.abbrev`, the auto-scaling minimum length as a repo grows, and
  what happens when an abbreviation goes ambiguous. Also `@{-1}`, `HEAD~`, and refnames as
  the "don't type a hash at all" escape hatch.
- **Sapling / Mercurial** — local sequential revision numbers alongside global hashes, and
  why Mercurial ultimately regretted them.
- **`gh` and Linear/Jira** — short sequential keys, and what coordination they pay for it.
- **`beads` / `seeds`** — named in Appendix A as the design ancestors; what they do here.

For each, record the mechanism, the ambiguity behaviour, and the cost. The output is
evidence, not a recommendation.

**Resolved when** each tool's mechanism is written up with sources, and the trade-offs are
stated in terms that the prefix and title-resolution tickets can consume directly.

set.title: Should rp resolve a ticket from an id prefix?
set.body:
## Question

Should `rp` accept a **prefix** of a ticket id wherever it accepts an id — `rp show jdt`
resolving `jdt9c2` — and if so, under exactly what rules?

This is the direct answer to "hard to type", and the seam is clean: `normalize_id` in
`ids.py` is the single chokepoint every command already funnels through. But the details are
where it lives or dies:

- **Minimum length.** One character is unusable; three is git-ish. Does the floor scale with
  ticket count, as git's does, or stay fixed?
- **Ambiguity.** The map's standing constraint says a hard `exit 1`. Confirm that, and decide
  what the error *says* — listing the candidate titles turns a failure into the search the
  human actually wanted.
- **Interaction with the display prefix.** `RP-jdt` — does the rendered form accept
  abbreviation too? `normalize_id` currently splits on the last `-` and demands exactly six
  characters after it.
- **Interaction with sync.** Does an abbreviation ever reach a remote, a shadow file, or the
  event log? It must not — the log stores bare ids (§5.2) — so confirm the resolution happens
  at the CLI boundary and nowhere deeper.
- **The agent-first tax.** Agents pass full ids and would now pay a lookup that can fail in a
  new way. Is the resolution cost real against a folded ticket set, and does it touch
  `rp ready`?

**Resolved when** the rule is stated precisely enough to implement, including the minimum
length, the ambiguity behaviour and message, and the boundary at which resolution happens.

set.title: Should rp resolve a ticket by title?
set.body:
## Question

Should `rp` resolve a ticket from its **title** — `rp show "compaction loses"` — wherever it
accepts an id?

This is the answer to the *other* half of the problem. Humans remember "the compaction bug",
never `RP-7hwnnt`, and the wayfinder skill's "Refer by name" rule already insists that
everything a human reads uses titles. If the skill hands the human a name and the tool only
accepts an id, the human is left doing the translation by hand — which is precisely the
friction that started this map.

The tension is that title matching sits awkwardly against agent-first determinism:

- Titles are **mutable**. An id is forever; a title changes under `rp set <id> title=...`, so
  a title reference can silently stop resolving — or worse, start resolving to something
  else.
- Titles are **not unique**, and matching is a spectrum: exact, substring, case-insensitive,
  fuzzy. Each step up is friendlier and less predictable.
- It **collides with prefix resolution**. If `rp show foo` can mean either an id prefix or a
  title substring, the grammar is ambiguous by construction. Options: a distinguishing sigil,
  a separate flag (`rp show --title "..."`), a search subcommand that prints ids rather than
  resolving them, or ruling one of the two out entirely.

Note the escape hatch: a *search* command that prints candidates and makes the human pick is
strictly weaker than resolution, but it is deterministic, cannot mis-resolve, and may cover
the recall moment completely.

**Resolved when** title-based addressing is either specified precisely (match semantics, tie
handling, how it is distinguished from an id) or ruled out with the reason recorded.

set.title: How a human starts a wayfinder session without typing an id
set.body:
## Question

How does a human start a `/wayfinder` session without typing an id at all?

This is the user's original complaint at its narrowest, and it may be answerable without
touching `rp`. The skill's "Work through the map" mode is invoked "with a map (URL or
number)" — but a Rohrpost map is not just any ticket: it is an **epic labelled
`wayfinder:map`**, which makes it findable by query. `rp list --label wayfinder:map --json`
already returns exactly the maps, and if there is only one open map the human need supply
nothing.

Decide:

- **The zero-argument case.** With exactly one open map, does `/wayfinder` just take it? That
  is the common case and removes the id entirely.
- **Disambiguation.** With several open maps, what does the human type? A number from a
  printed menu is typeable and unambiguous but positional and unstable across invocations; a
  title fragment is stable and memorable but overlaps the title-resolution question.
- **Pointing at a specific child ticket.** The skill lets the user name a ticket rather than
  taking the frontier's first. Same question one level down, but the candidate set is small
  and already scoped to the map, which makes cheap answers viable here that would not be
  safe repo-wide.
- **The doc surface.** Whatever is decided lands in the "Wayfinding operations" section of
  `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, which currently tells the agent to pass a map id around.

Watch the boundary: if the answer needs general title resolution in `rp`, this ticket has
grown into the title-resolution question and should defer to it rather than pre-empt it.

**Resolved when** the invocation contract is specified — what the human says to reach a map
and a ticket within it — and it is clear whether it needs anything from `rp` core.

set.title: What rp renders when a human, not an agent, is reading
set.body:
## Question

What should `rp` put on screen when the reader is a **human**, so that ids stay out of the
way?

The map holds that "hard to reason about" is a rendering problem, not an id problem: six
random characters will never be memorable, so the fix is to stop making a person look at
them. `rp` already has two audiences and one of them is explicitly served — `--json` is the
agent interface and "the plain output is for human terminals" — but the plain output has
never been designed *as* a human surface.

Make it concrete rather than arguing it. Prototype the human-facing rendering of the calls a
person actually runs by hand — `rp ready`, `rp list`, `rp tree`, `rp show` — and react to it:

- Where does the id belong: leading column, trailing dim text, or absent until needed?
- If prefix resolution lands, should the distinguishing prefix be visually marked, the way
  `jj` highlights the part you need to type? That turns every listing into a lesson in what
  is safe to type.
- `rp tree` is the map's whole-map view. Does an epic and its children read as a *map* today,
  or as a flat dump with indentation?
- Does anything here justify colour, given `NO_COLOR` is respected (§10)?

Keep it cheap and throwaway: static mock output pasted side by side is enough to judge, and
faster than wiring a renderer.

**Resolved when** a preferred human rendering exists as a concrete artifact, linked from this
ticket, with the reasoning for what was kept and what was cut.

text:
Resolved. Full write-up with sources: `docs/research/id-addressing-prior-art.md`.

**The mechanism every comparable tool converged on.** Prefix resolution is not a novel idea to
be weighed — it is what *every* surveyed tool with random ids and human users implements: jj,
git, Mercurial, Sapling, and beads. All of them treat ambiguity as a hard error, which
independently confirms the standing constraint this map already adopted.

**Findings that bear directly on the open tickets:**

- **jj scopes resolution.** `IdPrefixContext` resolves a prefix inside a configured revset
  first (defaulting to what `jj log` shows) and only falls back to the whole repository on a
  miss. Short prefixes therefore stay short, because unrelated history cannot lengthen them.
  The Rohrpost analogue — resolve within open tickets first, then all tickets — is a real
  option the prefix ticket did not anticipate. It costs context dependence: the prefix you
  need changes as the scope changes.
- **jj also renders the answer.** The default template shows at least 8 characters but styles
  the *distinguishing* prefix differently from the padding, so every listing teaches the
  reader how much they actually need to type. That is the tightest coupling found between the
  typing problem and the rendering problem.
- **git scales its floor.** `b = floor(log2 N)+1`, then at least `ceil(b/2)` characters, floor
  of 7 — a birthday bound, not a guess. It answers the "fixed or scaling minimum" question
  with a formula. Note Rohrpost's collision domain is ~2^30 over one repo, far smaller than
  git's object count, so the arithmetic differs even if the approach transfers.
- **git and beads both print the candidates** on ambiguity, with titles/subjects. Both judged
  it worth the code — it converts a dead end into the search the human wanted.
- **Title matching is never identity.** Not in a single surveyed tool. The two that offer it
  keep it in a separate, list-returning command (`sd search`), or make the multiple-match rule
  explicit and positional (`git :/regex` takes the youngest match). This is the strongest
  single signal in the survey and the title ticket should start from it.
- **Sequential keys always have an allocator.** GitHub, Linear, and Jira can afford `ENG-123`
  only because creation passes through one central service. Mercurial, which allocated locally
  instead, documents the result as a defect: revnums are "strictly local convenience
  identifiers" and "Do not use them to talk about changesets with other people." This is
  first-party confirmation of the out-of-scope call on this map — the alternative was tried
  and its own maintainers warn against it.
- **Seeds, the nearest ancestor, requires exact ids** and has no id completion at all. Its
  shell completion covers commands and flags only. So the ancestor does not solve this, and
  there is nothing to inherit.

reason: Prior art gathered in docs/research/id-addressing-prior-art.md: every comparable tool with random ids implements unique-prefix resolution with hard-fail ambiguity; no tool treats a title as identity.

Should `rp` accept a **prefix** of a ticket id wherever it accepts an id — `rp show jdt`

  small and already folded into memory.

  abbreviation too? `normalize_id` currently splits on the last `-` and demands exactly six

  message, ticket body, or map link — or a durable reference. If the former, say so where a
  human will read it.

behaviour and message, resolution scope, the boundary at which resolution happens, and
whether an abbreviation may be durably written down.

set.title: [addr] Human-addressable tickets: how a person points at a Rohrpost ticket
[addr-1] Which human moments actually require typing a ticket id?
[addr-2] How comparable tools make random ids addressable
[addr-3] How a human starts a wayfinder session without typing an id
[addr-4] Should rp resolve a ticket from an id prefix?
[addr-5] Should rp resolve a ticket by title?
[addr-6] What rp renders when a human, not an agent, is reading

text:
**No — and no alias field either.** Titles are **search keys, never identities**. The 6-char
base32 id remains the only identity a ticket has.

## What was decided

A human handle is encoded as a **leading bracketed prefix in the title**:

```
[addr-2] How comparable tools make random ids addressable
```

The prefix (`addr`) is agreed with the user when the map is charted; the sequence is
allocated by the charting session, which creates the tickets serially in one process. The
bare prefix `[addr]` titles the map epic itself, so `/wayfinder addr` reaches it.

`rp` learns **nothing** about this convention. No new field, no `SET_FIELDS` entry, no fold
change, no `_fieldts` entry, no `doctor` check, no uniqueness contract. The only tool change
is a general `rp search` over titles, which is justified independently.

## Why the title, and not a field

Rejected, in the order they were considered:

- **A dedicated `aliases: [...]` field.** Schema change, a new merge surface, and a new
  uniqueness contract for `doctor` to police — all of it unnecessary once titles carry the
  handle and search can find it.
- **An alias as a label.** Decisive objection: the GitHub provider maps `labels`
  bidirectionally (`providers/github.py:104-118`), so an alias label would sync to GitHub, be
  editable there, and fight the set-wise merge.
- **A repo-global prefix→id store.** Duplicate state — the ticket knows its handle and so
  does the file, so `doctor` gains a drift check that can fail — plus a brand-new git conflict
  surface unless it is append-only JSONL under `merge=union`. It also buys nothing for
  allocation, since "next free number" is a filter over already-folded tickets.

## Why clashes are safe

Two branches independently allocating `[addr-7]` is **not a corruption**. The ids stay
distinct and correct; two tickets simply have titles containing the same text. `rp` has no
uniqueness contract over titles to violate, so nothing to detect and nothing to repair at the
tool level. Search returns both rows; renumbering one is the fix.

This is the whole reason the handle must not be an identity. It is also why the clash window
is small in practice: a map's tickets are allocated serially in one charting session, so only
later additions can collide.

## Why substring search is exact

The brackets delimit, so no special matching logic is needed: `[addr-2]` is **not** a
substring of `[addr-20]` — the closing bracket differs. Plain substring search over titles is
therefore exact for handles, which keeps `rp search` dumb.

## Costs accepted

- **One handle per ticket.** A plural alias list would have allowed several; a second handle
  in a title pollutes it. Conscious YAGNI trade.
- **Titles are mutable and sync bidirectionally** under per-field LWW (§8.2), so an edit on a
  remote can win and silently drop the handle. A local-only field would have been immune.
  Bounded here: syncing is a deliberate maintainer action, not ordinary skill work, and map
  tickets are local planning artifacts. Must be documented rather than defended against.

## Corroboration

The prior-art survey ([addr-2]) found that **no** surveyed tool treats a non-id string as an
identity — title lookup is always a separate, list-returning search (`sd search` in seeds;
`git :/regex` makes its multiple-match rule explicit and positional). This decision was
reached independently and lands in the same place.

reason: No: titles are search keys, never identities. Human handles ride in the title as a leading bracketed prefix ([addr-2] ...); rp learns nothing but gains a general search.

set.title: [addr-7] Specify rp search
set.body:
## Question

What exactly does `rp search` cover, and what does it return?

The decision in [addr-5] made search the *only* tool change needed for human handles, which
puts weight on getting its surface right. No search exists today: `rp list` has fixed filters
(`--status`, `--label`, `--parent`, `--type`) and no free-text matching.

Settle:

- **Which fields.** Title alone is enough for handles and is the cheapest, most predictable
  option. Bodies and comments are where prose lives, and searching them is a different
  feature with a different cost — the fold holds bodies inline today (§13.2), so a body scan
  is not free. Decide whether this is `--in title,body` or title-only, and resist scope creep
  toward a general text index.
- **Match semantics.** Plain case-insensitive substring is enough to make `[addr-2]` exact,
  because the brackets delimit. Anything fuzzier (regex, token matching, ranking) buys
  nothing for handles and costs determinism, which the map's standing constraint values above
  convenience.
- **Output shape.** Same row shape as `rp list --json`, so agents parse one format. Confirm.
- **Composability with existing filters.** `rp search "[addr-" --parent <map>` is how a
  wayfinder session would enumerate a map's handles. Does search accept the `list` filters, or
  is it a separate, unfiltered command?
- **Exit codes.** Zero matches: `0` with an empty list, or `1`? §10 says non-zero on error,
  and "found nothing" is not an error — but a script distinguishing the two matters. Note
  `rp list` sets the precedent; follow it rather than inventing.
- **Whether `list` absorbs it instead.** A `--match <text>` flag on `rp list` is strictly less
  surface than a new command and inherits every filter for free. This is the KISS option and
  should be beaten, not assumed away.

**Resolved when** the surface is specified precisely enough to implement and to write into
§10: fields covered, match semantics, output shape, filter composition, and exit codes —
including the possible answer that this is a flag on `rp list` rather than a command.

set.title: [addr-8] What wayfinder does when two handles clash
set.body:
## Question

What does a wayfinder session do when two tickets carry the same handle?

[addr-5] established that a clash is safe — the ids stay distinct, `rp` has no uniqueness
contract over titles, and nothing is corrupt. That makes this purely a **skill behaviour**
question, and the skill has to answer it because nothing else will: no `doctor` check will
ever fire, so an unhandled clash simply sits there until it confuses someone.

Settle:

- **Detection.** A session already lists the map's children to find the frontier, so it can
  spot duplicate handles in the same pass. Is that check worth making explicit in the skill,
  or does it only run at allocation time (when picking the next free number)?
- **Allocation under concurrency.** "Next free number is max+1" is what a charting session
  does naturally. Two branches adding a ticket later both take `N+1`. Is anything cheap worth
  doing here — leaving gaps, or deriving the number from something already unique — or is
  accepting the rare clash the correct KISS answer?
- **Repair, and who loses.** Renumbering one side needs a deterministic tiebreak so two
  agents repairing concurrently reach the same answer. Ticket `created` timestamp is the
  obvious candidate; ids sort deterministically too. Pick one and say why.
- **Dangling references.** A renumbered handle may already be written into the map's
  Decisions-so-far, a commit message, or a PR comment. Map bodies are editable; commit
  messages are not. Decide whether repair rewrites the references it can reach, and what the
  skill tells the human about the ones it cannot.
- **Where it is written down.** The user asked for this to live in the Rohrpost
  documentation, agent-first: `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` (Wayfinding operations) and the
  installable skill in `skills/skills/rohrpost`. Note that an installed copy of the skill can
  drift from the repo — that staleness problem is out of scope here and sits in the map's fog.

**Resolved when** the skill's clash behaviour is specified — detection point, allocation rule,
deterministic tiebreak for repair, and reference handling — and the wording is ready to drop
into the tracker doc.

## Destination

A locked decision on **how a human addresses a Rohrpost ticket**, recorded as an ADR plus an
amendment to spec §5.1 (Identifiers) and §10 (CLI), ready to hand to a build session. The
decision, not the code: implementation is handed off once the way is clear.

## Notes

**Domain.** Rohrpost's id/addressing ergonomics, driven by `/wayfinder` being awkward to
drive by hand: `RP-jdt9c2` is hard to type and impossible to hold in your head.

**Skills.** Call `grilling` and `domain-modeling` every session. Use `research` for facts
outside this repo. No `CONTEXT.md` exists yet — create one when the first term is resolved.

**Plan, don't do.** The destination is a decision, not shipped code. One explicit exception,
granted by the user: `rp search` is authorised to be built once the handle convention has
been dogfooded on this map.

**Handles.** This map dogfoods its own decision ([addr-5]): every ticket carries a leading
bracketed handle, `[addr-N]`, and the map itself is `[addr]`. Refer to tickets by handle plus
title; the 6-char id stays the identity.

**Standing constraints, settled while charting:**

- **Agent-first holds** (`AGENTS.md`). Human affordances live on the *input* side only — what
  `rp` accepts. What agents emit and consume does not change; `rp ready --json` stays fast
  and small (§10).
- **Ambiguity is a hard error** (`exit 1`), never a guess. Determinism is worth more to an
  agent than convenience is to a human. *(Confirmed by prior art: every comparable tool does
  exactly this.)*
- **The stored id form is fixed** at 6 lowercase base32 chars (§5.1). Only the *addressing
  layer* is in play — what `rp` accepts as input and what it renders.
- **"Hard to type" and "hard to reason about" are two problems.** Typing is input
  ergonomics. Reasoning is a rendering-and-prose problem: 6 random characters can never be
  memorable, so the fix is to keep bare ids out of the human's face, not to make them
  prettier.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket; zoom the link for the detail it holds -->

- **[addr-2] How comparable tools make random ids addressable** (`RP-twaq4c`): every tool with
  random ids and human users (jj, git, hg, Sapling, beads) implements **unique-prefix
  resolution with hard-fail ambiguity**, and **no** tool treats a title as identity — title
  lookup is always a separate, list-returning search. Write-up:
  [`docs/research/id-addressing-prior-art.md`](docs/research/id-addressing-prior-art.md).
- **[addr-5] Should rp resolve a ticket by title?** (`RP-keswrj`): **No**, and no alias field
  either. Titles are **search keys, never identities**. Human handles ride *in* the title as a
  leading bracketed prefix — `[addr-2] ...` — with a per-map prefix agreed at charting time.
  `rp` learns nothing about the convention; the only tool change is a general search. Clashes
  are safe precisely because the handle is not an identity: two tickets sharing `[addr-7]` is
  a duplicate string, not a corrupt id.

## Not yet specified

- **The write-up itself**: which ADR, and the exact §5.1 / §10 wording. Waits on the
  remaining addressing mechanism ([addr-4]) being settled.
- **Shell completion**: whether it is part of the answer, and for which shells. None exists
  today, and neither does it in `seeds`. Waits on the moments audit.
- **A positional handle** over the last result set (`rp show @2` against `rp ready`). Waits
  on the moments audit and on the rendering question. Note this overlaps [addr-5]'s handles —
  it may already be redundant.
- **Doc staleness for installed skills**: `skills/skills/rohrpost` ships with the repo, so an
  installed copy drifts from the tool it documents. Making `rp` self-documenting would fix it,
  but that is a different effort from addressing and would widen this map past its
  destination.

## Out of scope

- **Changing the stored id form** — sequential numbers, counters, or title-derived slugs.
  Spec §5.1 rejects these deliberately: they need either central coordination (which this
  design exists to avoid) or mutability. The prior-art research closed this off further:
  every tool with short sequential keys (GitHub, Linear, Jira) pays for a central allocator,
  and Mercurial, which allocated locally instead, warns in its own docs that the result must
  not be used to talk to other people. Reopening this would redraw the destination, and that
  is a fresh effort, not a resumption.
- **Handles as a synced field.** Considered and dropped while resolving [addr-5]: an alias
  carried as a label syncs to GitHub bidirectionally and would be editable there. Handles stay
  local, inside the title.

set.title: [addr-7] Specify the search surface

text:
**A `--match` filter on `rp list`, not a `rp search` command.** Shipped.

## The surface

```
rp list --match <text>
```

- **Fields covered: title only.** Bodies are held inline in the fold (§13.2), so scanning them
  is not free, and prose search is a different feature with a different cost. Handles and
  titles are what a human recalls; that is what `--match` covers.
- **Match semantics: case-insensitive substring.** Nothing fuzzier. Regex, tokenising and
  ranking buy nothing for handles and cost determinism, which this map values above
  convenience. Plain substring is already *exact* for handles because the brackets delimit
  ([addr-5]).
- **Output shape: unchanged.** `--match` is a filter like any other, so rows are the same
  shape agents already parse.
- **Composes with every existing filter**, which is the whole reason it is a flag:
  `rp list --match "[addr-" --parent <map-id> --json` enumerates one map's handled tickets.
- **Exit code: `0` with an empty result.** Finding nothing is not an error; `rp list` already
  set that precedent and it was followed rather than re-litigated.

## Why a flag beat a command

`rp search` was the name in play throughout the discussion, but a separate command either
duplicates the four existing filters or does without them — and a search that cannot be scoped
to a parent or a status is not much use for finding one map's tickets. The flag inherits all
of them for free and adds no new command to the CLI surface (§10). KISS/YAGNI, per
`AGENTS.md`.

## Implementation

One predicate in `api._list_predicates`, the existing chokepoint every filter already funnels
through, plus the argparse flag and a pass-through in `cmd_list`. No new module, no new
concept in the data model.

Three tests in `tests/test_api.py`, one of them a regression test for the bracket-delimiting
property that the entire handle convention rests on: `[addr-2]` must not match `[addr-20]`.

Docs updated: spec §10, `docs/users/README.md`, `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, and the
installable skill.

Verified against the live map: `rp list --match "[addr-2]"` returns exactly one ticket, and
`rp list --match "[addr]"` returns exactly the map epic.

reason: Shipped as 'rp list --match <text>' (case-insensitive title substring) rather than a separate rp search: a flag inherits every existing filter, a command would duplicate them.

set.title: [win] Windows-native rohrpost: rp + skills without WSL
set.body:
## Destination

`rp` runs natively on Windows (CPython 3.14 via uv/uvx), the test suite is green on a `windows-latest` CI leg, and every `rp`-touching skill works from PowerShell, cmd, and Git Bash — no WSL. POSIX behaviour unchanged.

## Notes

- Plan-don't-do is overridden for the `wayfinder:task` tickets: execution is carried inside this map; the destination is a delivered change.
- Work each task ticket in its own branch/worktree; commit every green increment; merge to main once green.
- Windows install root for the local wrapper defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\rohrpost`; `ROHRPOST_HOME` keeps precedence.
- Settled decisions shaping every ticket: all three shells in scope (PowerShell/cmd/Git Bash); `--body-file` replaces heredoc teaching; skill docs = inline Windows sections + one shared Windows playbook; spec §7 rewritten to the invariant (mechanism as implementation note); locking = platform split (`msvcrt`/`fcntl`), no new dependencies.
- `rp`-touching surfaces in scope: the `rohrpost` skill, `setup-repo-skills` (its Rohrpost tracker template), `babysit-pr`, and this repo's `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket: [title](link): gist -->

## Not yet specified

- Whatever the Windows CI leg exposes beyond the locking fix — temp-file, permission-bit, or path assumptions elsewhere in `src/`. Cannot be phrased sharply until [win-9] has run.

## Out of scope

- Developing rohrpost itself on Windows (Makefile targets, mutation runs stay POSIX-first).
- Standalone `.exe` distribution (uvx / local wrapper is the install path).
- WSL as a support target.

set.title: [win-1] research: msvcrt locking semantics for a blocking exclusive lock
set.body:
## Question

`store.file_lock` is today `fcntl.flock` (exclusive, blocking, per open file description, callers must not nest). What does `msvcrt.locking` actually provide on Windows, and what must a blocking exclusive lock on `.rohrpost/.lock` look like in CPython 3.14?

Pin down, each claim to a primary source (Python docs, CPython source, Microsoft docs):

- lock granularity: byte-range on the `.lock` file — which range, and does the file need nonzero length?
- lock scope: per file handle vs per process; what happens on a second handle in the same process?
- `LK_LOCK` retry behaviour (tries, interval) vs `LK_NBLCK`/`LK_RLCK`; unlock (`LK_UNLCK`) requirements
- blocking loop shape: is `LK_LOCK`'s built-in retry sufficient, or spin on `LK_NBLCK` with backoff?
- crash behaviour: are locks released when the holding process dies?
- interaction with `lock.open("a+", encoding="utf-8")` (text mode, append) and `msvcrt.locking`'s fd requirements

Resolved by the `research` skill: findings to `docs/research/windows-file-locking.md`, every claim carrying its source link.

set.title: [win-2] research: uv + Python 3.14 on Windows runtime facts
set.body:
## Question

Which runtime facts about uv and CPython on native Windows do the wrapper, playbook, and CI work depend on? Primary sources only (uv docs at astral.sh/docs, Python on Windows docs, GitHub uv releases):

- `.venv` layout after `uv sync` on Windows: where does the `rp` console script land (`Scripts/rp.exe`? `rp-script.py`?), and how do the shims behave from PowerShell, cmd, and Git Bash?
- `uvx rohrpost` on Windows: resolution, cache location, first-run latency characteristics
- install-root convention: is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<app>` the idiomatic cache-style home (vs `%APPDATA%`, `%USERPROFILE%`)?
- gotchas: WindowsApps `python.exe` execution aliases, MAX_PATH/long-path behaviour for deep `.venv` trees, OneDrive/defender interference worth warning about

Resolved by the `research` skill: findings to `docs/research/windows-uv-runtime.md`, every claim carrying its source link.

set.title: [win-3] research: Git for Windows vs a committed JSONL event log
set.body:
## Question

Which Git-for-Windows behaviours threaten a committed JSONL event log (`.rohrpost/log.jsonl`) or the sync merge path, and which `.gitattributes`/config choices fix them? Primary sources only (git-scm docs, gitforwindows.org, Git source where needed):

- `core.autocrlf` defaults across Git-for-Windows installer choices; what a CRLF working tree does to our `open(..., "r")`/`strip()` reads and to `os.write` appends
- effect of `text eol=lf` attributes on `.rohrpost/**/*.jsonl`: round-trip identity for a repo checked out on both OSes; do the existing `merge=union` rules interact with CRLF?
- is `git merge-file` present in typical Git-for-Windows installs (incl. minimal/PortableGit)? `core.longpaths` default and impact

Resolved by the `research` skill: findings to `docs/research/windows-git-jsonl.md`, every claim carrying its source link.

set.title: [win-4] Windows locking design for file_lock
set.body:
## Question

Settle the design [win-1] informs, precisely enough that [win-7] implements it verbatim:

- which byte range of `.lock` gets locked, and the lock-file lifecycle (created once, never deleted?)
- blocking: `LK_LOCK`'s built-in retry vs a spin on `LK_NBLCK` with backoff; total wait and failure mode
- re-entrancy: the docstring's "callers must not nest" contract — still true under `msvcrt`?
- what `doctor` says about a stale `.lock`
- the POSIX/Windows seam in `store.py`: guarded top-level import vs per-platform helper modules; how tests fake/verify each side

set.title: [win-5] --body-file CLI contract
set.body:
## Question

Herdedoc-free multi-line bodies for every shell. Settle the contract [win-8] implements:

- which commands grow `--body-file` (`new` certainly; `comment`? `set` body? `resolve`?)
- `-` reads stdin; interaction/precedence with `--body` and `--template` (error or last-wins?)
- error modes: missing file, empty file, undecodable bytes — exit code and message shape
- docs to touch (`docs/users`, SKILL.md examples) so the heredoc teaching gets a portable sibling

set.title: [win-6] Spec §7 rewrite: invariant over mechanism
set.body:
## Question

Rewrite spec §7 so the contract is the invariant — appends serialised under an exclusive advisory lock; a partial line never lands; readers tolerate a torn tail — with per-platform mechanisms (fcntl.flock / msvcrt.locking, O_APPEND semantics incl. the Windows story) as implementation notes, not contract. Existing tests must still map 1:1 onto the reworded guarantees. Blocked by [win-1] so the Windows mechanism's real atomicity story is stated truthfully.

set.title: [win-7] Implement platform-split locking in store.py
set.body:
## Work

Per [win-4]'s decision: replace the top-level `import fcntl` with the platform seam; `msvcrt.locking` path for Windows (byte-range on `.lock`, blocking per design), `fcntl.flock` elsewhere byte-identical. `append_event` untouched. Tests cover the Windows path (CI leg proves it for real) without weakening the POSIX concurrency tests. `pyproject.toml`'s `Operating System :: OS Independent` claim becomes true.

Per [win-5]'s contract: add `--body-file` (and stdin `-`) to the settled commands with the agreed precedence and error modes; tests for each. Update `docs/users` and the SKILL.md examples so every heredoc teaching gains a portable sibling.

set.title: [win-10] eol=lf protection for .rohrpost JSONL
set.body:
## Work

Per [win-3]'s findings: `paths.GITATTRIBUTES_RULES` gains `eol=lf` (or `text eol=lf`) for `.rohrpost/**/*.jsonl`; the shipped repo's own `.gitattributes` gets the same rules; `rp init` writes them idempotently as today. Decide (small, inline) whether `doctor` warns when an existing repo lacks the rule. Verify round-trip: a repo checked out on Windows with `autocrlf=true` folds identically.

set.title: [win-11] rohrpost skill Windows pass: wrappers + playbook
set.body:
## Work

- `.ps1` and `.cmd` wrapper templates mirroring `rohrpost.template`: validate install, resolve `.venv/Scripts/rp(.exe)`, default home `%LOCALAPPDATA%\rohrpost`, honour `ROHRPOST_HOME`; never bypass the wrapper.

- New shared Windows playbook (install: uv, clone, `uv sync`, wrapper materialisation, validation); `playbooks/install-local.md` points to it for Windows instead of duplicating.
- Wrapper self-test: extend `test-rohrpost-wrapper.sh` for Git Bash only if cheap; otherwise note it.
